newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh grain harvest seen far below forecast.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh grain harvest seen far below forecast.

text.p: Kazakhstan's grain harvest, important to hungry markets like Russia, will probably fall far below official forecasts, industry sources said on Wednesday.

Crop specialists at the Academy of Agricultural Sciences, who declined to be identified, said 1996 net grain output in the former Soviet republic would slip to 11 million tonnes, well below official predictions of 13-14 million tonnes.
"Grain in cleaned weight will total 11 million tonnes this year," one of the specialists said.

The Central Asian republic's government has periodically revised downward its outlook for 1996 output. Early predictions of 18 million net tonnes were cut to 16.5 million and then to 13-14 million last month.
Agriculture specialists said Kazakhstan could have little to export and could see domestic demand outstrip supply.

Kazakhstan would have enough grain to meet human demand, but that livestock levels could fall further against tight feed grain supplies, they added. Kazakhstan could seek to import some feed grains from former Soviet republics.

The impact on Kazakhstan's economy would probably be mild, since many exports are carried out on a barter basis. The country, rich in mineral and hydrocarbon resources, is relying on its precious metals and oil and gas sectors, not agriculture, to fuel economic recovery.
Deputy Prime Minister in charge of agriculture Zhanybek Karibzhanov said earlier this month that Kazakhstan hoped to export at least five to six million tonnes of grain from its crop this year.
"For them to export this much, they need at least a net harvest of 13-14 million tonnes," said independent agriculture specialist Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd in Moscow.
"They are not going to get that harvest," he said, adding that rains which had swamped Russian crops in Siberia had also affected northern Kazakh crops.
Kazakhstan plans to use about 2.5 million tonnes of grain for seed this year. Three million tonnes are used for food grain, while five million tonnes are fed to livestock.
One million tonnes will be used as barter payment to farmers, while two million tonnes go to state reserves.

The numbers, cited by the academy specialists, add up to 13.5 million -- a 2.5 million deficit against the 11 million tonne forecast. "We're going to be living from hand to mouth," one of the specialists said.

Kazakhstan's net, drought-hit 1995 harvest was officially 10 million tonnes. But independent specialists have said that actual output was probably three million tonnes higher and that producers underreported output to hoard stocks.
The academy specialists said disruptions in Russian electricity supplies to northern Kazakhstan had caused grain on some farms to spoil because it could not be dried and put into silos in time.
They said that drought-like conditions in the south and west had also hit crops, pushing yields in some places down to 0.2 tonnes per hectare.
Kazakhstan's harvest is nearly over and the government will announce a final figure in the first 10 days of November.

Nearly 70 percent of Russia's total wheat and wheat flour imports came from Kazakhstan over the 1995/96 crop marketing year. Russia, facing its own poor net harvest of around 70 million tonnes this year, is likely to continue to seek Kazakh supplies.
But grain sources in Moscow said that some small lots of Kazakh grain was moving fast to other Central Asian buyers such as Turkmenistan and Tajikistan.
"Kazakhstan may have something left over to sell, but the Central Asian states are moving in fast," said Alexander Yushik of Russia's Grain Union.
